claims.statement: Controlled human trial evidence specific to sermorelin/GHRH(1-29) in adults is limited: a small 1997 trial (11 healthy men, 64-76 years, 6 weeks of single nightly GHRH(1-29) injections) found improvement in only 2 of 6 strength measures and one muscle-endurance measure, with no change in DEXA-measured lean mass or fat, weight, BMI, or waist-to-hip ratio; a separate 2006 trial (89 healthy older adults, 6 months of daily GHRH treatment) found improved cognition on some measures (novel problem-solving, psychomotor/processing speed, working memory) but no improvement on 3 of 6 cognitive tests and no effect on sleep. Neither trial supports general anti-aging, well-being, insulin-sensitivity, or libido claims, and both are old, small, and use GHRH(1-29)/sermorelin rather than the compounded products currently marketed. Consumer-health reporting on sermorelin itself states that adult studies are limited and that definitive research supporting anti-aging benefits is lacking.

claims.statement: Sermorelin is popularly marketed online as a 'pro-aging support therapy' that 'restores your body's natural hGH production' and may increase general well-being, lean body mass, insulin sensitivity, and libido. The libido, insulin-sensitivity, general-well-being, and 'restores natural hGH production'/anti-aging framing are not supported by any controlled human trial identified for sermorelin/GHRH(1-29). The lean-body-mass claim specifically is also not supported: the one located controlled trial that measured body composition (Vittone et al. 1997, 11 elderly men) found no change in DEXA-measured lean mass or fat, though it did find improvement on 2 of 6 strength measures and one muscle-endurance measure. A separate controlled trial (Vitiello et al. 2006, 89 older adults) found improved cognition on some measures, which is not among the marketing claims evaluated here. None of this rises to evidence for the marketing claims as stated, and sermorelin's sole historical FDA-approved indication was pediatric growth hormone deficiency, now discontinued; these marketing claims should not be read as proven benefits.

conflicts.summary: Direct-to-consumer and compounding-pharmacy marketing pages frequently present sermorelin as a legitimate, clinically endorsed anti-aging/wellness therapy, while the confirmed regulatory record shows no FDA-approved sermorelin product currently on the market (DailyMed returns no results) and only sparse adult human trial evidence; this gap between marketing framing and the documented regulatory/evidence record is unresolved pending a dedicated review of individual vendor claims against updated FDA compounding status.
